newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish shares soar, attracting foreign interest.
newsitem.headline: Turkish shares soar, attracting foreign interest.

text.p: Turkish shares soared further into record territory on Monday as hopes of accelerated privatisation after last week's vital court ruling on Turk Telekom's sell-off drew new interest from foreign investors, analysts said.
The main Istanbul index, the IMKB National-100, ended the day up 13.11 percent from Friday's close at a record 1,700, and compared with an intraday high of 1,727.
The gains were accompanied by strong volumes, with a total 69.48 trillion lira ($602 million) traded, compared with a record 64.87 trillion lira ($562 million) on Friday.
Since the start of the year the index has risen 74.2 percent, or 61.5 percent in dollar terms. Last year, the index rose 143.8 percent and 35.8 percent in dollar terms.

Alongside optimism over privatisation, the rise has been driven by lower money market and bond market rates, a quiet currency market, prospects for 1996 corporate earnings and improving inflation data.
Analysts said there were increasing signs of buying interest from international investors eager to latch on to the upward momentum.
"There is heavy cash entry into the market. What is notable is the buying by brokerages known to deal with foreigners," said Huseyn Istanbullu of Meksa Securities.
Turkey has been the best performer in the IFC index of emerging markets so far this year.

The surge of interest in Turkish shares came in the wake of a constitutional court ruling last Thursday in favour of Turk Telekom's sale, which is expected to raise $3.5 billion in the initial offering slated for the second half of the year.
The Telekom revenue forecast outstrips the total income from sell-offs since Turkey initiated its privatisation programme over 10 years ago.

"When the Telekom company is listed it increases international interest substantially simply because it increases the market (capitalisation) and investors have to allocate more money for a bigger market," said Atilla Yesilada, director of research at Global Securities.
He said the Telekom sale would add $12-20 billion to a current market capitalisation of $40 billion.
However, international investors are wary of the breakneck speed of the gains since the Telekom decision, analysts said.

"It is true that foreign investors were buying during the latest rally. But they think that this sharp rise is not so healthy. So they may leave the market soon," said Oner Ayan from the institutional sales division of Ata Securities.

The gains have been so dramatic that many are beginning to question how much further the rally can go. Brokers said several shares again hit their upper 10 percent price margins for the morning session amid strong demand.

Of the 239 shares traded, 227 rose, four fell and eight closed steady. Among most active shares were utilities Aktas Elektrik and Cukurova Elektrik, largely-state-owned flat steel maker Eregli, and Turkish Airlines.

For the gains to continue beyond the short-term analysts say they are still looking for more from the government on serious structural reforms on the social security system and tax collection improvements.
Turkey's finance minister last week cited an improvement in tax collection in the latter half of 1996 as a factor in the better-than-expected deficit of 1,215 trillion lira ($10.6 billion).
Hopes for privatisation and other multi-billion dollar revenue raising schemes are the heart of the government's 1997 balanced budget plan.

The Telekom sell-off and a series of smaller privatisations, including three state banks and the leasing of several ports, will not alone guarantee a turnaround in the country's economic fortunes, analysts said.
The government must also push ahead with its aims to sell big petroleum and steel companies if it is to reach a target of $5 billion from sell-offs this year.
($1=115,300 Turkish lira)
